Jimmy, the small Deucalion job finished. It's verifier-only, run on FlashProve's own stored example proofs (synthetic weights), on one EPYC 7742 node with GCC 13.3, repo at 9e2bdd8f unmodified:

- Small stored proof: YES, 1.8 s, 157 MB
- Full-size proof (Maverick shape, 1,001 tokens, ~19 MB): YES, 23.5 s on one thread, 3.3 GB peak; 20.3 s with -j 64 (threads only split the longest stage)
- Its result line is identical, field for field, to the one in their README (same commitment ID, 128 bits with 32 bits of proof of work, tokens 24..1023). So their published verdict reproduces exactly on unrelated hardware.
- Negative controls: one flipped byte gives "NO: proof-refused"; a wrong commitment ID gives "NO: model-statement, nothing checked"
- Toy proofs: honest copy accepted, bit-flipped copy refused

What it doesn't show: anything about a served model (synthetic weights). Also, the printed bits are the C++ verifier's own accounting, while the Lean proof covers their Lean verifier, not cp_verify. They say so themselves.

Not run yet: the ARM cross-check and their CPU test suite. Those, and the zkIE comparison, wait for your plan.

Jimmy, one more heads-up so nothing surprises you tomorrow. After the first results I ran a second verifier-only round, still on FlashProve's own stored proofs and still nothing that touches zkIE or the comparison design:

- Tamper controls on the claim itself: change the answer token, or one prompt token, and the proof is refused (NO: reply-differs / proof-refused), including on the full-size proof
- Same checks on the ARM A64FX nodes: identical result lines to x86, so the verdict doesn't depend on the CPU
- Their CPU test suite: 78 passed, nothing falsely accepted; the 8 failures all come from Deucalion's old OS (glibc 2.28, kernel 4.18), at build, link or harness steps

Great work Merlini. A published verdict that reproduces field for field on unrelated hardware, with the tamper controls failing the way they should, is exactly the evidence this space is short of.

We added a third machine: built cp_verify unmodified at 9e2bdd8f on our own server and checked the small stored proof. YES in 2.6 s, and 27 of the 28 fields match the published result line (the 28th is the build digest, a placeholder in their README). A flipped byte gives NO: proof-refused, a wrong commitment ID gives NO: model-statement. Merlini, if your unmodified build printed build=93afdaf5…9595, that matches ours too.

Two more things:

1. On the IP boundary Jimmy raised: FlashProve is Apache-2.0 (with a NOTICE file; the parts it adapts from ggml are MIT), unlike DeepProve's non-commercial terms. So adapting its approach in zkIE looks open as long as the attribution is kept. We haven't audited every file, so it's worth a proper check before anything ships.

2. On Pavlo's point, gates not scores: agreed. A valid inference proof says this output came from this committed model. It says nothing about where the input came from, whether an action on it was authorised, or that what ran is what was proven. We wrote our check up as a signed record that says exactly that: what was checked, the commands and digests to repeat it, and which gates it does and doesn't cover, verifiable without trusting us:
https://github.com/babyblueviper1/invinoveritas/tree/main/examples/inference-proof-record

We'll do the same for the zkIE side of the comparison once Jimmy has a plan, so both sides report in one format.

Great work. Once Jimmy has the FlashProve/zkIE comparison plan ready, I'd like to bring VECA into the discussion as well.
We already implemented native zkIE proof verification, cryptographic bindings across provenance, model, judgment and execution records, plus a claim-aware authorization engine with independent admission recomputation.
The experiments include negative cases and mutation controls showing where valid component proofs fail to authorize stronger downstream claims.
It's not an LLM-scale proving benchmark, but it could be useful for evaluating what guarantees actually survive beyond inference verification.
We can compare these boundaries once Jimmy's methodology is ready.

Thanks all. Two answers and one correction on the unit, since it matters for the plan.

Fede: yes, our unmodified build printed build=93afdaf5…9595 too, on both x86 (EPYC 7742) and ARM (A64FX). Same digest across three machines.

Jimmy, on "a single token": it depends on the run. Their route 4 on the real Maverick weights proves one token, but the stored full-size proof we verified covers 1,001 output tokens in one proof: positions 24 to 1023 of a 1,024-token request plus the next token, each checked as the token the committed model ranks first (greedy). The covered: line in the verifier output names the range. It's proved after the fact over a given sequence, in one prefill-style pass, which is where their ~110 tokens/s "prefill" figure comes from. So I'd align on "output positions covered per proof" and "proved after generation vs during it", rather than tokens vs whole output. Agreed on GPU vs CPU: their prover only runs on an H100, while our numbers so far are verify-side, on CPU.

Pavlo: VECA alongside makes sense, and gates, not scores: our README already lists what a YES does and doesn't establish, and Fede's record does the same, so the comparison can start from those.

Thanks Jimmy, clear write-up. I'd back the CPU route, with three suggestions so the result holds:

1. Let their unmodified verifier referee the port. Whatever we port, its proofs must come back YES from the unmodified cp_verify at 9e2bdd8f, and the tamper controls (answer token, prompt token, proof byte, commitment ID) must still come back NO. Otherwise we'd be benchmarking our port, not FlashProve. We already have those checks scripted on Deucalion, so that part is ready.

2. It may be less of a port than it looks. blocks/ is a plain C++17 prover and verifier for every block of the protocol, building without CUDA, and its heavy steps sit behind one interface (engine/engine.h) with a CPU implementation (engine_cpu.h). The GPU prover has its own EngineGpu. What's CUDA-only is the model-specific part (attention and the rest, 36 .cu files under prover/). So the route might be "their CPU engine plus rewriting the model kernels" rather than a full rewrite. Worth confirming as you read. I'd stage it: their 8-layer synthetic model first, full size only once that passes the verifier.

3. Align the request shape, not just "one token". A FlashProve run proves a range of positions plus the next token: the stored full-size proof covers positions 24–1023 plus the next token in one proof. It can be set to one position, so let's pick the same (prompt length, checked positions) for both systems and record it next to every number.

On "their edge is CUDA tuning, not crypto": that's exactly what a same-hardware run would tell us, so I'd leave it as the hypothesis the benchmark tests. Two practical notes: Deucalion has plenty of CPU time for this (about 47k x86 core-hours, plus ARM, until 31 Dec) and A100 hours if we ever go route 2. And a port is a derived work under Apache-2.0, so we keep their NOTICE and mark the files we change. Pavlo's gates apply throughout: each number goes next to what the proof does and doesn't guarantee.

Our FlashProve check is the first row, and a small stdlib script validates any row:

Jimmy, a three-way with DeepProve makes sense, and Fede's row format looks like the right common ground: one row per number, with the referee's commit and result line next to it. Three things worth settling before anything is forked:

1. DeepProve's licence is stricter than non-commercial. Its LICENSE (Lagrange, 2024) grants a personal, non-transferable licence to use it internally, only for testing and evaluating, and to use an unmodified version (§2). §4 rules out reproducing, distributing, publicly displaying or making derivative works, and transferring it to any third party. As I read it, a fork in the Trustless AI org, private or not, and modifications for controlled testing would both be outside that. Benchmarking it unmodified, with each of us installing it ourselves, looks like what it allows. Publishing its numbers isn't addressed directly, so it may be worth asking Lagrange before the report goes out. That's my reading of the text, not legal advice. FlashProve is the opposite case: Apache-2.0, so a fork and a CPU port are fine, keeping their NOTICE and marking changed files.

2. If any runs use Deucalion, the published report needs the grant's credit line: "Compute for this work was provided on Deucalion (CNCA/FCCN) under project 2026.00071.INOVIA.VERTICECRIATIVO, awarded by FCT through the BSC AI Factory." It's a condition of the allocation for anything public, the same line as on the booth card. Running the benchmark there is within the allocation's described work, so no extra approval is needed.

3. FlashProve's issues are open, but the README says it's unmaintained and not accepting contributions, so a short issue linking to the report is about right. Worth knowing: another group (giskard09) posted there on 3 Nov, with an example chaining a FlashProve proof into an on-chain record of the agent's action.

On our side, we can run the verifier jobs on Deucalion (x86 and ARM) for whatever proofs the benchmark publishes, and add rows in Fede's format to the flashprove-checks repo, so each number gets a check on another machine.

Good idea, and it's exactly what 8274's IProofVerifier layer is for. One constraint shapes it: a FlashProve proof is big. The stored full-size proof is 18.78 MB, and even the small example is 4.1 MB. At 16 gas per non-zero calldata byte, just sending the full-size proof is around 300M gas, several blocks' worth, before any verifying. So I don't think cp_verify itself can run in a contract. Three routes that fit 8274, from soonest to hardest:

1. Commitment registry first. FlashProve says the commitment ID must come from a party you trust, never from the prover. An on-chain registry of commitment IDs, with who published each, is small, useful straight away, and every route below needs it.

2. Attestation paradigm, available now. Independent verifiers run the unmodified cp_verify and sign the result: commitment ID, request hash, answer, and the result-v1 line's digest. Fede's signed rows already do this. An IProofVerifier with proofSystem "attestation" checks k-of-n of those signatures. Honest about its trust model: you trust the verifiers, and anyone can re-run them.

3. True ZK on-chain, later. Wrap FlashProve's verification in a small SNARK whose proof a contract can check cheaply. That's the only way to the "zk" paradigm, but it's a large piece of work, and the soundness of the wrapper has to be argued on top of FlashProve's own.

An optimistic version of 2 (post the claim with a bond, and anyone can recompute within a window) is a middle ground. Happy to help spec 1 and 2 in the fork.

One more piece for this, which we have in hand: a friend from the ethscriptions side, Jeff (jefdiesel), built ChunkTech, an open tool (MIT, npm "chunktech") that stores files on-chain as chunked calldata. It splits a file into 33 KB pieces, stores them on Base, can put a pointer on Ethereum mainnet, and checks the SHA-256 when it reassembles them. His demo serves an 8 MB PDF from about 200 chunks.

For FlashProve that solves where the proof lives. By his cost figures, the full-size proof (18.78 MB) is about 750 chunks, roughly $1.50 on Base, and the small one about $0.35. Combined with the routes above, that's a complete version we could build now:
1. the commitment ID in an on-chain registry;
2. the proof stored on Base with ChunkTech, its hash recorded;
3. independent verifiers running the unmodified cp_verify on those exact bytes and signing the result, checked by an 8274 IProofVerifier (attestation).

Anyone can then fetch the proof and re-run it without trusting a server. One precision: the chunks live on Base, which hands its data to Ethereum only as short-lived blobs, so it's "stored on Base, pointer on Ethereum", not "on Ethereum".

Links: https://chunktech.chainhost.online · github.com/jefdiesel/chunktech

A proposal for a new primitive. I'd like the group's OK before opening a repo.

What: recomputable chunked storage. Storing a file on-chain as chunked calldata, so anyone holding the file computes exactly the same chunks and manifest, and anyone holding the transaction hashes can fetch, reassemble and check it against an on-chain root. No server to trust.

Why now: the inference-proof benchmark. FlashProve proofs are 4–19 MB. Stored this way, with the commitment ID in a registry and independent verifiers signing their cp_verify results, every published number gets proof bytes anyone can re-check. It's the storage half of the ERC-8274 attestation route.

Where it comes from: ChunkTech by Jeff (jefdiesel), an open MIT tool already doing chunked calldata storage on Base with a pointer on mainnet. I asked Jeff first: he's happy to help build it, and credit to ChunkTech is part of it either way.

What the primitive would add:
1. a byte-exact spec for chunking and encoding;
2. a manifest with a Merkle root over the chunks, recorded on-chain;
3. conformance vectors with negative controls (reordered, missing or truncated chunk must fail);
4. a recompute-kit step: tx hashes in, verdict out.

The spec and our implementation would be CC0 like everything else here, with ChunkTech credited as its origin. Honest numbers: Jeff sees $10+ for 19 MB on Base at current gas, and the data lives on Base with a pointer on Ethereum, not on Ethereum itself.

Timing: after Web Summit (12 Nov). Questions for the group:
- OK to add it as a Trustless AI primitive?
- Any objection or overlap with something that already exists?
- A name? I'd suggest chunked-calldata.
- Who'd like to be involved?

I'm supportive of this as a Trustless AI primitive, provided we keep the scope narrow and reuse the existing recompute-kit anchor boundaries.
One issue worth addressing first: ChunkTech currently generates a random chunk ID, so identical input bytes don't necessarily produce identical encoded chunks.
I'd define a deterministic, domain-separated manifest, bind the ordered chunk hashes and transaction references, and distinguish byte reconstruction from authenticated on-chain inclusion.
We should also keep storage verification separate from FlashProve verification and ERC-8274 authorization.
"chunked-calldata" works as a name. I can help review the spec and negative controls after Gate A.

Thanks Pavlo, agreed on all of it, and you're right on the chunk ID. I checked the published code (chunktech 0.3.0): generateChunkId() makes a random 16-byte ID whenever none is passed in, and the cross-chain manifest also carries a Date.now() timestamp, so neither is reproducible from the bytes. The helpful part is that chunkData() already accepts an ID as a parameter, so an ID derived from the file's own hash fits Jeff's API as it is.

So the scope, as you put it:
1. Narrow, reusing recompute-kit's existing anchor boundaries.
2. A deterministic, domain-separated manifest binding the ordered chunk hashes and the transaction references. Nothing random, no timestamps.
3. Two separate claims, verified separately: byte reconstruction ("these chunks rebuild exactly this file") and authenticated on-chain inclusion ("these bytes are in these transactions on this chain").
4. Storage verification only. FlashProve verification and ERC-8274 authorization stay outside it and just consume its result.

Name: chunked-calldata. Timing: after your review, and after Web Summit for the build. I'll leave this open to the others until Friday, then open the repo if there are no objections, and let Jeff know about the determinism point.

hey team — a quick one from the FlashProve deep-dive that I think ties in nicely with our zkIE LogUp work.

We found where a big chunk of FlashProve's speed comes from, and it's structural, not just good engineering. In their lookup argument, the lookup tables are never committed. All the non-linear function tables (softmax/exp, SiLU gate, sigmoid, rotary, plus the range tables) are public and fixed: the verifier regenerates the four float tables locally, bit-for-bit, and checks every table against digests carried in the config (tsilu0..7, tsig0..7, trope0..7, texp0..7). So the tables cost the prover nothing — no commit, no opening, no OOD. What actually gets committed is only the hidden key side and the multiplicity planes.

This lines up exactly with what we measured on zkIE's Batch LogUp: the dominant cost was opening commitments (144 witness columns → 4 batched commitments + one batch opening gave us the ~4-5x), not building the table mapping. FlashProve simply deletes that dominant cost class by keeping tables public-and-fixed.

Takeaway for us: wherever our lookup tables are public and derivable (gelu/rsqrt/softmax over fixed ranges), committing and opening them is pure overhead we can avoid the same way. Worth noting too: our earlier fix of actually committing the lookup tables was about soundness, not performance — FlashProve shows the sound path is making the table publicly fixed + digest-anchored, not handing it to the prover.

One more idea to poke at for the ERC-8274 on-chain verifier: generating those lookup tables in-contract at verify time, so the contract stays compact without any table commitment. Gas and float ops on-chain are open questions — need to look into it. Will share once we dig deeper.

Route 2 works for us, and we can be one of the n from the first FlashProve row: we'll put our signing key and its fingerprint in flashprove-checks beside our rows, and sign each row against the fork's exact commit.

One rule worth fixing in the IProofVerifier spec early: a signature counts toward k only under a key the contract lists in advance, and never one held by the prover or by whoever published the commitment ID. Otherwise k-of-n can be met by one party with n keys. It's the same independence rule the work-acceptance record just settled on: the relying party has to get the verifier's key from outside the claim itself.
